rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
F = k q₁q₂/r²
E = F/q
∮E·dA = Q/ε₀

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ treat "Electric field due to point charges" as one blob → ✅ split into: electric field due to point charges, field lines.  ·  ❌ state the rule without its limit → ✅ note when it applies / stops applying.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Coulomb: F = (1/4πε₀)·q₁q₂/r². Electric field E = F/q = kq/r²; for a line/dipole use superposition.  ·  Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ — powerful for spherical/cylindrical/planar symmetry.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Electric field intensity.** The field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there: E = F/q₀ = (1/4πε₀)q/r² for a point charge, directed away from a positive charge.  ·  **Field lines.** These imaginary lines are drawn so that the tangent at any point gives the field direction and their density shows field strength.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Potential V = kq/r; ΔV = W/q; U of a charge in potential = qV. Equipotential surfaces are ⟂ to field lines.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Field line rules.** Lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, never cross each other, and never form closed loops in electrostatics.  ·  **Uniform field.** Between two parallel oppositely charged plates the field is uniform (E = V/d), so a charge experiences the same force everywhere between the plates.  ·  **Superposition.** The total field from several charges is the vector sum of their individual fields — the same principle that gives the net force.
